heroText: Tallinn is Estonia's compact capital, where medieval walls, Baltic ferries and digital-era energy sit close together. Start in Tallinn Old Town, climb to Toompea Hill for viewpoints, then walk Telliskivi Creative City or the Seaplane Harbour for a newer side of town. Tallinn Airport is close, making short city breaks unusually easy.

areas.name: Tallinn Old Town
areas.text: Old Town is the classic first base, with medieval lanes, restaurants, viewpoints and most sights within walking distance.

areas.name: Rotermann Quarter
areas.text: Rotermann Quarter has modern hotels, restaurants and design shops between Old Town, the harbour and business areas.

areas.name: Telliskivi
areas.text: Telliskivi is the creative district for cafes, bars, street art and a more local evening base.

areas.name: Kadriorg
areas.text: Kadriorg is quieter and greener, close to the palace, art museums and seaside walking routes.

airports.name: Tallinn Airport (TLL)
airports.text: Tallinn Airport is southeast of the centre and connects quickly by tram, taxi and bus.

airportTransfer.value: 15-25 min by tram, taxi or bus to central Tallinn
airportTransfer.distance: about 4 km southeast of the centre

stayOverview: Stay in Tallinn Old Town for the classic first visit, Rotermann Quarter for modern hotels and harbour access, Telliskivi for cafes and nightlife, or Kadriorg for green space and museum-focused days.
hotelIntro: Tallinn is small enough that walking works well, but the mood changes by district. Old Town is atmospheric, Rotermann is practical and polished, Telliskivi is social, and Kadriorg is calmer and greener.
rentalCars: Do not rent for central Tallinn; use a car only for Lahemaa, bog walks or wider Estonia trips.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Old Town for a first short stay, or Rotermann if you want newer hotels near the harbour.

travelTips.title: Airport tram
travelTips.text: Tallinn Airport is close enough that tram and taxi transfers are both simple for most central hotels.

travelTips.title: Winter
travelTips.text: Winter streets can be icy and dark, so pack warm footwear and plan indoor museum breaks.

travelTips.title: Day trip
travelTips.text: Lahemaa National Park is the classic nature day trip for bogs, manor houses and Baltic coast scenery.

highlights.name: Tallinn Old Town
highlights.title: Tallinn Old Town
highlights.text: Tallinn Old Town preserves medieval walls, lanes, churches and squares in one of the Baltic region's strongest historic cores.

highlights.name: Toompea Hill
highlights.title: Toompea Hill
highlights.text: Toompea Hill adds outdoor time to a Tallinn stay, with open space, views or waterfront breathing room between denser city sights.

highlights.name: Telliskivi Creative City
highlights.title: Telliskivi Creative City
highlights.text: Telliskivi Creative City is a named stop in Tallinn worth keeping on the route when it fits the day's transport, timing and neighborhood plan.

highlights.name: Seaplane Harbour
highlights.title: Seaplane Harbour
highlights.text: Seaplane Harbour adds the water-facing side of Tallinn, making it a good break from museums, traffic and dense historic streets.

highlights.name: Kadriorg Palace
highlights.title: Kadriorg Palace
highlights.text: Kadriorg Palace anchors a green museum district and park east of the centre, built for Peter the Great.

highlights.name: Balti Jaam Market
highlights.title: Balti Jaam Market
highlights.text: Balti Jaam Market is useful for reading Tallinn's daily rhythm through food stalls, craft sellers, local errands and short stops between bigger sights.

history.label: 19th century
history.text: The 19th century brought industrialisation of the city and the port kept its importance.
It was followed by German occupation until the end of World War I in November 1918, after which Tallinn became the capital of independent Estonia.
During World War II, Estonia was first occupied by the Soviet army and annexed to the USSR in the summer of 1940, then occupied by Nazi Germany from 1941 to 1944.

During the most devastating Soviet bombing raid on 9–10 March 1944, more than a thousand incendiary bombs were dropped on the city, which caused large-scale fires, as a result of which 757 people were.
Tallinn became the capital of a de facto independent country once again on 20 August 1991.
The Old Town became a World Heritage Site in 1997, and the city hosted the 2002 Eurovision Song Contest.
Tallinn was the 2011 European Capital of Culture, and is the recipient of the 2023 European Green Capital Award.
